captions.instagram:
What are work and power?

Pull a crate at an angle, wind a bucket up a well, and watch the joules pile up under a graph. Race up the stairs at 350 watts, meet Watt's horse, lift a rice sack with a lever, pulley and ramp, read your electricity bill in kilowatt-hours, and find out why holding still makes you tired but does no work.

→ Work is force times distance: pull 200 newtons for 5 metres and you do 1,000 joules.
→ Pull at an angle and only the part along the motion counts: W = F d cos θ.
→ Hold a bucket still and you do no work on it, however tired your arm gets.
→ A 60 kg student running up 3 metres in 5 seconds works at about 350 watts.
→ Watt timed mill horses: 33,000 foot-pounds a minute. One horsepower is 746 watts.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/workclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: What are work and power? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Pull a crate at an angle, wind a bucket up a well, and watch the joules pile up under a graph. Race up the stairs at 350 watts, meet Watt's horse, lift a rice sack with a lever, pulley and ramp, read your electricity bill in kilowatt-hours, and find out why holding still makes you tired but does no work.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/workclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/workclear

In this video:
• Force times distance. You do work when a force moves something along its direction: W = F × d, in joules.
• Power is a rate. Power is work ÷ time, in watts.
• Machines trade force for distance. Levers, pulleys, ramps and gears let a small force do a big job, but only by moving further.
• Paying for work. Electricity is sold by the kilowatt-hour: 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ.
• Myths and limits. Carrying a bag level does no work on it: the force is at 90° to the motion.
